title: Golgi versus Ramon y Cajal and the neuron doctrine
text:
CHAPTER 4. THE NEURON AND THE SYNAPSE
SECTION 4.1. GOLGI VERSUS RAMON Y CAJAL AND THE NEURON DOCTRINE

What is the brain made of?

By the middle of the nineteenth century, scientists knew that nerves carry electrical signals and that different parts of the cortex do different things. But they did not know what the basic building blocks of the nervous system were, or how they were connected. This was a serious gap. Imagine trying to understand a computer knowing only that it uses electricity and that different chips do different things, but without knowing about transistors or how wires connect them.

The cell theory, developed in the late 1830s by Matthias Schleiden for plants and Theodor Schwann for animals, and extended by Rudolf Virchow's principle that every cell comes from another cell, held that all living things are made of cells. But nervous tissue was hard to fit into this theory. Under the microscopes of the time, it looked like a tangled mass of fibers and cell bodies, and it was impossible to see where one cell ended and another began. Nerve cell bodies had been described (for example by Jan Purkinje in the 1830s, who described the large cells of the cerebellum now named after him), and anatomists such as Otto Deiters in the 1860s had distinguished, in isolated cells, one long process (the axon, which Deiters called the axis cylinder) from multiple branching processes (the dendrites, then called protoplasmic processes). But how these processes related to each other across the tissue was unclear.

The reticular theory

The dominant view in the 1870s and 1880s was the reticular theory, associated especially with Joseph von Gerlach. It held that the nervous system is a continuous network (reticulum) of fibers. In this view, the fine branches of nerve cells fuse with each other to form a continuous mesh, so that the nervous system is a single connected structure, a syncytium, rather than a collection of separate cells. Signals would flow through this network the way water flows through a network of pipes, or current through a mesh of wires.

This theory had some appeal. It seemed to explain how signals could spread widely through the nervous system. And with the staining methods of the time, the fibers really did seem to merge.

Camillo Golgi and the black reaction

Camillo Golgi (1843 to 1926) was an Italian physician and scientist. In 1873, while working in a small hospital for chronic patients in Abbiategrasso, near Milan, with a simple laboratory set up in a kitchen (as the story is often told), he discovered a new staining method. He hardened pieces of nervous tissue in potassium dichromate and then soaked them in silver nitrate. The result was a dark precipitate of silver chromate that formed inside some nerve cells. Golgi called it the "reazione nera," the black reaction. Today it is known as the Golgi stain.

The remarkable thing about the Golgi stain is that it stains only a small fraction of cells, apparently at random, but stains those cells completely, including their cell body, dendrites, and axon, in black against a pale yellow background. Why it stains only a few percent of the cells is still not fully understood. But this selectivity is what makes it so powerful. If every cell were stained, the tissue would be a solid black mass. Because only a few are stained, each stained cell stands out in full detail, like a single tree seen against an empty sky.

Golgi used his stain to describe many types of nerve cells and their branching patterns. He distinguished two main types of neurons by their axons: cells with long axons that leave the local region (now called Golgi type I neurons), and cells with short axons that branch locally (Golgi type II). He also discovered the Golgi tendon organ, a sensor of muscle tension, and, later, the Golgi apparatus, an organelle found in nearly all cells.

But Golgi interpreted his images within the reticular framework. He believed that dendrites were mainly for nutrition, taking up nourishment from blood vessels and glial cells, and that axons branched and fused into a continuous diffuse network through which nerve signals traveled. He never abandoned this view.

Santiago Ramon y Cajal

Santiago Ramon y Cajal (1852 to 1934) was a Spanish physician and histologist. As a boy, he wanted to be an artist, and his father, a professor of anatomy, pushed him toward medicine. He served as an army doctor in Cuba, where he contracted malaria and tuberculosis, and later became a professor in Valencia, Barcelona, and Madrid. He was a superb draftsman, and his drawings of neurons, many of them preserved at the Cajal Institute in Madrid, are among the most beautiful scientific images ever made.

In 1887, Cajal was shown preparations made with Golgi's method in Madrid by the neuropsychiatrist Luis Simarro. He was immediately impressed. He improved the method in two key ways. First, he used a "double impregnation" technique that gave more reliable staining. Second, and more importantly, he studied the nervous systems of embryos and young animals, especially birds. In young tissue, the axons are not yet covered in myelin (which can interfere with the stain), and the neurons are smaller and less densely packed, so that whole cells and their connections can be seen more clearly. Cajal compared this to studying a young forest, where the trees are smaller and more widely spaced, rather than a mature forest where the branches are entangled.

In 1888, Cajal published his first major findings, in a journal he founded and financed himself, based on studies of the bird cerebellum. He saw that the axon terminals of one cell came very close to the cell bodies or dendrites of other cells but did not fuse with them. The cells were separate. They communicated by contact, not continuity.

Over the following years, Cajal studied almost every part of the nervous system: the retina, the spinal cord, the cerebellum, the cerebral cortex, the hippocampus, the olfactory bulb, and many more. He produced a massive work, Textura del sistema nervioso del hombre y de los vertebrados (published in parts between 1899 and 1904), later expanded in a French translation as Histologie du systeme nerveux de l'homme et des vertebres (1909 to 1911). His observations led him to two great principles.

The neuron doctrine

The first principle is the neuron doctrine, which can be summarized as follows:

1. The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
2. Neurons are individual cells, separated from each other by their membranes, not fused into a continuous network.
3. Neurons have three main parts: dendrites, a cell body (soma), and an axon.
4. Neurons communicate with each other at specialized points of contact.
5. The neuron is a trophic (nutritional) unit: if an axon is cut from its cell body, the separated part degenerates. (This was shown earlier by Augustus Waller in 1850 and is known as Wallerian degeneration.)

The name "neuron" was coined in 1891 by the German anatomist Wilhelm von Waldeyer, who wrote an influential review summarizing the evidence, mostly Cajal's, for the independence of nerve cells. The neuron doctrine had several supporters besides Cajal, including Wilhelm His and August Forel, who reached related conclusions from developmental and degeneration studies. His showed that axons grow out from individual embryonic nerve cells, and Forel observed that degeneration after injury was confined to particular cells.

The law of dynamic polarization

Cajal's second great principle was the law of dynamic polarization. He proposed that signals flow through each neuron in one direction: from the dendrites and cell body, which receive inputs, to the axon, which carries the output to other cells. He arrived at this conclusion by studying the anatomy of systems where the direction of signal flow is known. In the retina, for example, signals must flow from the photoreceptors toward the optic nerve and brain. In the olfactory system, from the nose toward the brain. In the spinal cord motor system, from the cord out to the muscles. In each case, he saw that dendrites face the input side and axons face the output side.

Cajal later refined the principle slightly, noting that inputs can arrive directly on the cell body, and stating that signals flow from the receiving parts (dendrites and soma) to the axon. The principle allowed him to draw arrows on his circuit diagrams, showing the flow of information through networks of neurons. This was a huge step: it transformed the nervous system from a tangle of fibers into a set of circuits with directed connections, like a schematic diagram.

The 1906 Nobel Prize

In 1906, Golgi and Cajal shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine "in recognition of their work on the structure of the nervous system." It was an odd pairing, because they disagreed fundamentally about what that structure was. In his Nobel lecture, Golgi used the occasion to defend the reticular theory and to criticize the neuron doctrine. Cajal, in his own lecture, presented the evidence for the neuron doctrine. The two men were reported to have had a cool relationship. It is one of the most famous episodes in the history of the Nobel Prize: two scientists honored for the same method, drawing opposite conclusions from it.

Who was right?

Cajal was right, in the main. The final proof came only in the 1950s, when the electron microscope made it possible to see the synaptic gap directly. Electron microscopy studies, including those by George Palade and Sanford Palay and by Eduardo De Robertis and H. Stanley Bennett in the mid-1950s, showed that at chemical synapses, the membranes of two neurons are separated by a gap of about 20 nanometers (the synaptic cleft), with small vesicles clustered on the presynaptic side. The neurons are not continuous.

But nature is never as tidy as a doctrine. Golgi was not completely wrong. Some neurons are directly connected by gap junctions, also called electrical synapses. At a gap junction, channels made of proteins called connexins (in vertebrates) span the membranes of two neighboring cells, creating a direct pathway for ions and small molecules. Electrical current can pass directly from one cell to the next. Gap junctions are found in many parts of the nervous system, for example between some inhibitory interneurons in the cortex, where they help synchronize activity, and in the retina. So the nervous system does have continuous connections in some places. It is a network of separate cells, mostly connected by chemical synapses, with some electrical links.

Cajal's law of dynamic polarization also has exceptions. Some dendrites release neurotransmitters (dendrodendritic synapses, for example in the olfactory bulb), and action potentials can propagate backward from the axon initial segment into the dendrites (backpropagating action potentials), where they play a role in learning. Some neurons, such as certain cells in the retina, lack a classic axon entirely. But as a first approximation, the principle holds, and it remains the starting point for drawing neural circuit diagrams.

Glia

Golgi and Cajal also studied the other main type of cell in the nervous system, the glial cells, or glia (from the Greek for glue). Rudolf Virchow had introduced the concept of "neuroglia" in the 1850s as a connective substance. The Golgi stain showed that glia are cells with distinct shapes. Cajal and his students, notably Pio del Rio Hortega, classified glia further: astrocytes (star-shaped cells that support neurons and regulate the chemical environment), oligodendrocytes (which form myelin in the central nervous system), and microglia (immune cells of the brain). For a long time glia were thought of as mere support. Today we know they actively participate in brain function: astrocytes regulate synapses and blood flow, microglia prune synapses during development, and oligodendrocytes adjust myelination in ways that may affect learning.

The ratio of glia to neurons in the human brain was long said to be about ten to one, but careful counting using a method called isotropic fractionation, developed by Suzana Herculano-Houzel and colleagues, suggested that the human brain contains about 86 billion neurons and a roughly similar number of non-neuronal cells, so the ten-to-one figure appears to be a myth.

Cajal as a theorist

Cajal was more than an anatomist. He speculated on how the brain might learn, proposing that learning might involve the growth of new connections between neurons or the strengthening of existing ones. This idea anticipates Hebb's rule and the modern concept of synaptic plasticity. He also wrote about the "neuronal forest," compared the brain to a garden, and wrote a famous book of advice for young scientists, Reglas y consejos sobre investigacion cientifica (Advice for a Young Investigator), which is still read today.

Bridge to AI: from neurons to nodes

The neuron doctrine is the foundation for every neural network model. The idea that the brain is made of discrete units, connected by directed links, is exactly how an artificial neural network is structured: nodes (units) connected by weighted edges, with information flowing in a defined direction. Cajal's circuit diagrams, with arrows showing the direction of signal flow, are the ancestors of the computational graphs used in deep learning frameworks.

Cajal's law of dynamic polarization corresponds to the forward pass in a neural network: inputs come in, are combined, and output goes out. But note the exceptions. In the brain, signals can also flow backward into dendrites (backpropagating action potentials), and these backward signals help drive learning. This is intriguing because the main learning algorithm for artificial networks, backpropagation, also requires sending error signals backward through the network. In artificial networks, this backward pass is computed separately, using the same weights in reverse. Whether and how the brain does anything similar is a major question, discussed in chapter 7.

The reticular theory also has a modern echo. Some researchers have argued that thinking of neurons as isolated units misses important aspects of brain function, such as electrical coupling through gap junctions, the effects of electric fields generated by many neurons together (ephaptic coupling), and the slow chemical signaling through the extracellular space by neuromodulators. Artificial neural networks are pure "neuron doctrine" networks: discrete units, discrete connections. Brains have additional, more continuous channels of communication.

Finally, the Golgi stain's trick of labeling only a few cells is echoed in modern neuroscience tools. Techniques such as "Brainbow," developed in the lab of Jeff Lichtman and Joshua Sanes around 2007, use genetic methods to label individual neurons in many different colors, so that many cells can be distinguished at once. In connectomics, machine learning algorithms segment and trace every neuron in a volume of tissue from electron microscope images. Cajal traced neurons by eye and drew them by hand; today we train convolutional networks to do the same, at a scale he could never have imagined.

Summary

- Before the 1880s, the reticular theory held that the nervous system is a continuous network of fused fibers.
- In 1873 Camillo Golgi invented the black reaction, which stains a small fraction of neurons completely.
- Santiago Ramon y Cajal improved the method and used it on young tissue, showing that neurons are separate cells that communicate at points of contact, the neuron doctrine.
- Cajal proposed the law of dynamic polarization: signals flow from dendrites and soma to the axon.
- Golgi and Cajal shared the 1906 Nobel Prize while disagreeing about the basic structure of the nervous system.
- Electron microscopy in the 1950s confirmed the synaptic gap; gap junctions show that some neurons are directly connected.
- The neuron doctrine underlies all artificial neural networks; exceptions like backpropagating action potentials connect to questions about learning.
